title: Commutes Sentence of Michael Harris
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Michael Harris as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: On January 19, 2021, President Donald Trump commuted Michael Harris’s sentence, according to the Justice Department’s clemency list. DOJ identifies Harris as a Central District of California defendant sentenced to 235 months in prison and five years of supervised release for cocaine distribution offenses. The public list records the commutation but does not state the reduced term or why Harris was selected.
description_long: The Justice Department’s clemency list records President Donald Trump’s January 19, 2021 commutation of Michael Harris’s federal sentence. It identifies Harris’s case as originating in the Central District of California and lists an original prison term of 235 months, followed by five years of supervised release. The listed convictions concern a conspiracy to possess and distribute cocaine, aiding and abetting possession with intent to distribute cocaine, and possession with intent to distribute cocaine. A commutation changes a sentence; it does not erase a conviction or itself establish innocence. The public DOJ summary confirms the clemency action and identifies the sentence and offenses, but it does not specify how much punishment Trump removed, whether Harris was released immediately, or what rationale was given for this individual grant. Those limits matter because the list groups many grants and does not provide the underlying case file or a detailed explanation of the decision.

preserved_fields.title: Commutes Sentence of Michael Harris
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Michael Harris as part of a clemency list.

notes: The DOJ list identifies the original sentence and cocaine offenses but does not state the revised term or a case-specific rationale.

title: Commutes Sentence of Jodi Lynn Richter
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Jodi Lynn Richter as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: On January 19, 2021, President Donald Trump commuted Jodi Lynn Richter’s sentence, according to the Justice Department’s clemency list. DOJ identifies her as a defendant in North Dakota and lists a 179-month prison term, amended by a February 2016 court order, plus five years of supervised release. Her listed offense was a controlled-substance distribution conspiracy. The entry does not give the commuted term or a reason for her selection.
description_long: The Justice Department’s clemency list records President Donald Trump’s January 19, 2021 commutation of Jodi Lynn Richter’s federal sentence. It identifies her case as being in the District of North Dakota and lists 179 months in prison, as amended by a court order dated February 29, 2016, followed by five years of supervised release. The listed offense is conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute and distribute a controlled substance. A commutation changes punishment while leaving the conviction in place; it is distinct from a pardon. DOJ’s list confirms the action and provides the original sentence and offense, but it does not state the revised term, whether the decision resulted in immediate release, or why Richter was included among the clemency recipients. The account can therefore describe the grant and the criminal case it affected, but it cannot responsibly attribute a personal, political, or policy motive to Trump without additional case-specific documentation.

title: GSA Clears Trump D.C. Hotel Lease Despite Conflict Concerns
description_short: The General Services Administration said Trump’s company remained in compliance with its Old Post Office lease despite conflict-of-interest criticism.
description_medium: On March 23, 2017, the General Services Administration said the Trump company remained in compliance with its lease for the Old Post Office building in Washington, where the Trump International Hotel operated. The decision came amid criticism that Trump’s private business interests conflicted with his presidency. The reported conclusion is clear, but the available linked pages do not explain the agency’s lease analysis.

preserved_fields.title: GSA Clears Trump D.C. Hotel Lease Despite Conflict Concerns
preserved_fields.description_short: The General Services Administration said Trump’s company remained in compliance with its Old Post Office lease despite conflict-of-interest criticism.

notes: Needs context: the supplied linked pages are general GSA references, not documentation of the March 23, 2017 lease determination. The record lacks the agency statement, lease terms or compliance rationale needed for an accurate long explanation.
proposed_correction: Keep the event only with an event-specific GSA statement or contemporaneous report; otherwise narrow the entry to the documented general conflict concerns and remove the claim that GSA cleared the lease.

title: Ordered to Pay $2 Million in Trump Foundation Case
description_short: A judge ordered Trump to pay $2 million to settle a lawsuit alleging misuse of Trump Foundation funds.
description_medium: On November 7, 2019, New York Supreme Court Justice Saliann Scarpulla ordered Donald Trump to pay $2 million in damages in a case over the Trump Foundation. Her ruling addressed the charity’s use of funds in connection with Trump’s 2016 campaign. CNBC reported that more than $2.8 million raised by the Foundation had been used for the campaign and disbursed by campaign staff, although the money ultimately reached veterans’ charities.
description_long: The ruling came in a New York attorney general’s civil case alleging that Trump used the Trump Foundation to benefit his 2016 presidential campaign and engaged in other unlawful activity. Manhattan Supreme Court Justice Saliann Scarpulla relied on factual admissions in a final stipulation, finding that Trump breached his fiduciary duty to the charity and that waste occurred. The record, as summarized by CNBC, said more than $2.8 million raised by the Foundation was used for Trump’s campaign and disbursed by campaign staff rather than by the Foundation. The money ultimately went to the veterans’ charities for which it had been raised, but the judge ordered Trump to pay $2 million in damages, the amount that would otherwise have gone to the Foundation if it still existed. The Foundation had agreed to dissolve and donate its remaining funds. Trump disputed the attorney general’s characterization, but the reported payment followed the judge’s ruling, not a criminal conviction.
subcategory: Charity Fraud and Illegal Political Donations

preserved_fields.title: Ordered to Pay $2 Million in Trump Foundation Case
preserved_fields.description_short: A judge ordered Trump to pay $2 million to settle a lawsuit alleging misuse of Trump Foundation funds.

notes: CNBC reports the $2 million as damages ordered by the judge after factual admissions; this description distinguishes that ruling from a criminal conviction.

title: Trump Blames Shutdown for GDP Slowdown, Demands Lower Rates Online
description_short: After GDP slowed, Trump posted that the shutdown cost two points of growth and called for lower interest rates.
description_medium: On February 20, 2026, after reports that U.S. GDP growth had slowed in the fourth quarter, Donald Trump blamed the government shutdown for a two-point loss in growth and called for lower interest rates in a social media post. The reports describe the slowdown; they do not establish that the shutdown cost exactly two points.
description_long: The event is a presidential claim and policy demand, not an economic finding or a rate change. On February 20, 2026, Trump responded to reporting that U.S. economic growth had slowed in the fourth quarter by saying the government shutdown had cost two points of growth and by urging lower interest rates. The Reuters headline says the shutdown dented fourth-quarter growth, and the Associated Press headline describes the economy hitting the brakes. Neither report, as summarized in the record, supplies a GDP figure, a calculation, or the text of Trump’s post. The two-point figure therefore remains Trump’s claim rather than an independently established estimate. Interest-rate decisions are made by the Federal Reserve, so a presidential post can express pressure but does not itself change rates; no response or policy effect is documented here. The record also does not establish how much of the slowdown was caused by the shutdown rather than other economic factors.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Blames Shutdown for GDP Slowdown, Demands Lower Rates Online
preserved_fields.description_short: After GDP slowed, Trump posted that the shutdown cost two points of growth and called for lower interest rates.

notes: The two-point causal estimate is attributed to Trump; the supplied reporting does not provide an independent calculation or document a Federal Reserve response.
